list.listitem: Screening for Barrett's esophagus (BE) in the general population is not recommended; it is not addressed by the USPSTF. C
Screening for BE in high risk populations may be beneficial but clinical trials are lacking. C
Diagnosis is made by EGD with histologic confirmation. C
Treatment options for BE include surgery, endoscopic therapies and surveillance combined with reflux treatment; choice depends on degree of dysplasia, health of patient and patient preference. B
BE has a good overall prognosis as esophageal cancer is rare with a reported incidence of 0.33% per year. B

background.definition: Barrett's esophagus (BE) is defined by presence of columnar mucosa in the esophagus ≥1 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction with biopsy confirmation of intestinal metaplasia. Short segment BE involves less than 3 cm of the distal esophagus and long segment involves 3 cm or more.

list.listitem: Barrett's esophagus (BE) affects 1.6% of the population.
In a large population-based study, 2.3% with reflux symptoms and 1.2% of those without had BE.

A study identified 110 US Veterans (90% male, mean age 61 years) with no or minimal GERD symptoms undergoing colorectal cancer screening. When upper endoscopy was performed, they found that 7% had long-segment BE and 17% had short-segment BE.
Outpatient care costs approximately $1241/year.
Monthly medication use accounts for more than half of the total cost, with proton pump inhibitors accounting for 64.6% of total medication cost.
Medication cost per month in patients with Barrett's esophagus is similar to that in patients with diabetes mellitus.
Patients with BE reported below average quality of life compared with the general population.
Acid reflux is associated with an increased risk. See risk factor table.

Chronic acid reflux exposes the esophageal epithelium to acid causing chronic esophagitis. This tissue heals in a metaplastic process with abnormal columnar cells replacing squamous cells. This epithelium can then progress to dysplasia, ultimately leading to carcinoma.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history of BE or EAC

list.listitem: Screening for BE in the general population is not recommended by ACG or ASGE guidelines and is not addressed by the USPSTF.C
Screening for BE in high risk populations has not been studied in randomized trials. ACG and ASGE guidelines recommend that if it is considered, screen only selected patients at increased risk. B
Screening for BE in the general population is not cost effective and there are no validated strategies based on symptoms or other identified risk factors.

If screening endoscopy for BE is performed, limit to individuals with a family history of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) or BE, patients with sleeve gastrectomy and reflux, or patients with GERD and at least 1 additional risk factor (age >50 years, obesity/central adiposity, current or past history of smoking, or male gender). This recommendation was based on observational studies and expert opinion.

Several tools that incorporate these risk factors have been validated for predicting BE on initial endoscopy. They include the validated M-BERET and HUNT clinical prediction rules; the hyperlinks take you to those external calculators.

Screening in patients with reflux remains unproven due to high prevalence of reflux symptoms (40% of adults); extremely low rates of progression to cancer (estimated at 0.00039 cases per patient with reflux annually); and a lack of prospective studies demonstrating mortality benefits or decreased cancer mortality rates with screening endoscopy.

If screening is undertaken, the highest yield for BE is obtained in men age 50 years and older who have longstanding heartburn. Screening this population is also cost-effective costing between $10000 to $50000 per QALY saved compared with no screening or surveillance as long as surveillance is limited to patients with BE + dysplasia.
A clinical prediction rule that predicts erosive esophagitis, a major risk factor for BE, applies to Asian populations but has not been validated externally.
Weight loss, strenous exercise and smoking cessation may prevent BE, although clinical trial data are lacking.
Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) decrease the risk of developing dysplasia (ARR = 37%, NNT = 2.7; based on 10-yr incidence).

A recent large randomized trial found that high dose PPI (esomeprazole 40mg t) with aspirin (325 mg daily) prevented death, malignant transformation or histological progression in patients with BE and no high-grade dysplasia. 9% of patients taking aspirin plus high-dose esomeprazole compared with 14% of those taking aspirin plus low-dose esomeprazole (NNT = 20; 12-67) experienced the combined primary outcome.
Diagnosis is made by EGD with histologic confirmation. C
Patients with long segment BE and Caucasians are diagnosed more accurately. B

Diagnostic criteria for Barrett's esophagus: (1) endoscopic documentation of columnar epithelium lining the distal esophagus (≥1 cm), and (2) histologic confirmation of specialized intestinal metaplasia in biopsy of the columar epithelium.
If risk factors are present, consider diagnostic EGD (see risk factor list).

Otherwise, history and physical have little utility due to a high rate of asymptomatic patients (31%) and low rate of patients with reflux having BE. An Italian population-based study found that 1.3% of patients had BE, of whom 31% were asymptomatic. Endoscopic findings (esophagitis, BE, PUD, erosions, or neoplasia) were seen in 18% of asymptomatic persons, 25% with dyspepsia but no reflux, 30% with dyspepsia and reflux, 34% with reflux alone, and 35% with alarm symptoms or signs.
All patients with alarm symptoms should have prompt diagnostic work-ups (e.g., dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, or weight loss). The positive predictive value of an alarm symptom for cancer is 3%.

Endoscopy with histological confirmation is 90-100% sensitive for diagnosis of BE. With endoscopy, long-segment BE is more accurately diagnosed than short-segment BE (OR = 3.63). Caucasian patients are more accurately diagnosed than African American patients (OR = 3.63).
An observational study of 488 patients with low grade or non-dysplastic BE found that high grade dysplasia or cancer were found in 1.9% a year later.

Because low grade dysplasia is a predictor of neoplastic progression in BE, expert GI pathologist confirmation is recommended as best practice. As this is not always available and due to inter-observer variability, a risk prediction assay (TissueCypher Barrett’s Esophagus Assay) has been developed and validated to risk stratify patients with BE. The 68% sensitivity and 79% specificity of the assay for predicting progression to high-grade dysplasia/EAC are comparable to expert pathologist evaluations and detect 50%-56% of progressors who were downstaged by expert pathology review.
Capsule endoscopy has 67% sensitivity and 84% specificity, but is not cost-effective compared with standard EGD as a screening tool.

Chromoendoscopy involves applying chemical agents to improve the characterization of mucosal surface either by selective uptake (using methylene blue or Lugol's solution) or enhancement of mucosal surface pattern (contrast staining with indigo carmine and acetic acid). Studies demonstrate mixed results (no better or worse than random biopsies).

Narrow-band imaging is an electronic form of chromoendoscopy and combines high-resolution endoscopy with special light filters to produce detailed images of the mucosal and vascular surface patterns within the BE segment. This technique enables inspection of the mucosa and vascular patterns for irregularities and enables diagnosis of BE with fewer biopsies and also detects more areas with any dysplasia compared with regular endoscopy (30% vs. 21%, p=0.01). The BING criteria are a classification scheme used to identify high grade dysplasia and cancer.
The most recent American College of Gastroentrology (ACG) guidelines recommend using chromoendoscopy during surveillance in patients with BE.

Flow cytometry measures DNA content in fresh frozen plasma specimens of mucosa to predict cancer risk. Predictors of increased cancer risk include: high grade dysplasia; aneuploid; increased 4N fraction on flow cytometry. However, these tests are not currently available for routine clinical use.

A study compared usual care with use of a swallowed Cytosponge in patients with GERD in the primary care setting. The sponge was well tolerated, and detected BE in 2% of those screened (n = 140), of whom 4 had dysplasia and 5 had stage I esophageal cancer This compares with only 13 patients diagnosed with BE in the usual care group. We do not know if this detection improved clinical outcomes.

An additional case-control study using a swallowed Cytosponge used methylated DNA markers to identify BE. Median BE length was 6 cm and 50% had dysplasia. The sensitivity and specificity for this non-endoscopic test were 92% and 94% respectively (LR+ 15, LR- 0.08) for BE detection compared with endoscopy.The ACG endorses this test as an acceptable alternative to endoscopic screening for BE in patients with chronic reflux and other risk factors.

Another non-endoscopic test involves swallowing a small capsule attached to a catheter and using a syringe to deploy an esophageal balloon sampling device that is combined with a DNA-based screening assay. Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated at a single VA among veterans with GERD symptoms and at least 3 additional risk factors including white race, obesity, male sex, smoking history and family history of BE or EAC. The gold standard was sedated EGD performed after the balloon sampling. This test has demonstrated sensitivity ranging from 85% to 93% and and specificity of 72% to 85% for BE/EAC.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.

A validated clinical prediction rule identified patients at risk for progression to high grade dysplasia as males (9 points), smokers (5 points), BE length (1 point/cm) and confirmed low grade dysplasia at diagnosis (11 points). Annual rates of progression were 2.3% for scores >20; 0.73% for scores of 11 to 20 and 0.13% for scores of 0 to 10.
ACG and AGA guidelines recommend endoscopic ablation for patients with high grade dysplasia and BE. C

ACG and AGA guidelines favor endoscopic ablation for patients with low-grade dysplasia but surveillance is still a reasonable option when risks versus benefits are discussed with patients. A meta-analysis found less progression to HGD or EAC with ablation compared to surveillance (RR=0.25, 95% C.I.0.07-0.93).B
Recommended surveillance intervals after endoscopic ablation are expert based. See C

Pharmacotherapy is recommended for low-grade dysplasia and for high-grade dysplasia in combination with approaches described in surgical therapies below. The goal of therapy is to suppress stomach acid production with agents such as PPIs to control reflux symptoms. Standard doses of any one of the five available PPIs (omeprazole [20-40 mg daily], lansoprazole [15-30 mg daily], rabeprazole [20-40 mg daily], pantroprazole [40-80 mg daily], and esomeprazole [20-40 mg daily]) can be used and doses can be increased if symptoms aren't relieved.
Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy is associated with a significant reduction in the risk of developing dysplasia in patients with BE (ARR = 37%, NNT = 2.7; based on 10-yr incidence).

Chemoprevention is effective for BE with low-grade dysplasia. A recent large randomized trial found that high dose PPI (esomeprazole 40mg twice daily) with aspirin (325 mg daily) prevented death, malignant transformation or histological progression in patients with BE and no high-grade dysplasia. 9% of patients taking aspirin plus high-dose esomeprazole compared with 14% of those taking aspirin plus low-dose esomeprazole (NNT = 20; 12-67) experienced the combined primary outcome.

An observational study comparing PPIs with H2 receptor antagonists found significantly lower cumulative incidence of dysplasia among patients who received PPI after BE diagnosis compared to those receiving no therapy or H2 receptor antagonist (ARR = 25%, NNT = 4).
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.

See for an overview of surgical and endoscopic therapies. ACG and AGA guidelines recommend endoscopic ablation for patients with BE and high grade dysplasia, as well as those with T1a eophageal cancer. Ablation or surveillance are options for patients with low grade dysplasia.

Esophagectemy is an option in high-grade dysplasia, especially for appropriate surgical candidates. However, there are no studies demonstrating superiority over endoscopic techniques. A retrospective comparison study with 199 patients found similar long-term mortality at 5 years versus photodynamic therapy and endoscopic mucosal resection (9% for esophagectemy vs. 8.5% for endoscopic techniques). A Cochrane review identified 13 studies comparing endotherapy with surgery, but they did not meet inclusion criteria so firm conclusions could not be drawn.
Operative mortality is high in low-volume centers (20%); esophagectomy should be performed at centers performing at least 20 procedures annually, where mortality is 8.4% or less.
Complications including pneumonia, arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, heart failure, wound infection and anastamotic leaks affect 30% to 50% of patients.
Even minimally invasive techniques using laparascopy and thorascopy have not improved outcomes.

Mucosal ablation therapies are used in conjunction with acid suppression and include: photodynamic therapy, thermal ablation with argon plasma coagulation or multipolar coagulation, radiofrequency ablation and endoscopic cryotherapy.

Endoscopic mucosal resection involves excision of a large segment of esophageal mucosa down to the submucosa. This technique is recommended in high-grade dysplasia to resect areas of mucosal irregularity such as nodularity or ulcer and can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.

A large retrospective cohort of patients undergoing endoscopic ablation (across 60 US health systems) found low rates of progression to EAC (2.4%, 6 per 1000 patient years), esophagectomy (1.5%) and all-cause mortality (13 per 1000 patient years).

A Dutch observational study followed patients with low-grade dysplasia (n=375), high grade dysplasia (n=422) or low risk esophageal cancer (n=589). All underwent endoscopic resection of visible lesions and then radiofrequency ablation every 3 months until BE was completely eradicated. Follow-up was for a median of 43 months. The most common complication was mild-moderate esophageal stenosis. The likelihood of recurrence of dysplasia was only 1% per person per year.

Three small RCTs (n = 282) randomized patients with BE and low grade dysplasia to endoscopic surveillance or radiofrequency ablation. Follow-up endoscopy was performed at 6 and 12 months in the ablation group and then every 12 months in both groups. Patients were followed for 3 years in two RCTs and only 1 year in one RCT. Progression to high grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma occurred less frequently in the ablation group (5.3% vs. 24.2%, NNT = 5 for progression to either outcome). Harms including strictures; major bleeding requiring either blood transfusion, intervention, or hospitalization; perforation; and serious adverse events all occurred in the ablation groups (2.4%, NNH=42).
A Cochrane review found a single study evaluating pre-operative radiotherapy that showed a trend toward benefit.
Antireflux surgeries such as fundoplication are not more effective than pharmacotherapy for preventing cancer in patients with BE.
BE has a good overall prognosis as esophageal cancer is rare with a reported incidence of 0.33% per year.B
Annual progression to esophageal cancer risk in patients with high-grade dysplasia ranges from 7% to 19%, with higher rates seen when pathology is evaluated rigorously. B
Progression to esophageal cancer is rare in patients with BE with an incidence of 0.33% per year.
Risk factors for progression include longer duration or length of BE and for those with high grade dysplasia.

One study concluded that the rate of cancer in patients with long-segment BE is approximately 0.5%. However, a subsequent study of 1017 German patients with newly diagnosed esophageal adenocarcinoma concluded that the annual transition rate from Barrett's to cancer was 0.22% for long segment (>3 cm), 0.03% for short segment (1-3 cm) and only 0.01% for ultrashort segment (<1 cm).

A registry-based cohort study in Northern Ireland found a 5-fold increase in the risk for esophageal cancer in patients with BE, but no difference in all-cause mortality between patients with BE vs. the entire general population.

A Veteran's Administration cohort study of 324 men with BE found very low risk of progression to high-grade dysplasia or esophageal cancer if there was no dysplasia on initial endoscopy, or low-grade dysplasia and BE length less than 6 cm.

Another cohort study with 327 BE patients followed for a mean of 3.9 years found very low malignancy risk in patients with negative histology, low-grade or indefinite dysplasia, and neither aneuploidy or increased 4N on flow cytometry. If high-grade dysplasia, aneuploidy or increased 4N was found, there was much higher risk.

See algorithm in for a suggested approach to follow-up. Surveillance endoscopy is only supported by retrospective surgical series reporting a survival advantage based on earlier diagnosis, and thus are subject to lead time and length biases. ACG guidelines on surveillance are based on expert opinion with surveillance intervals based on presence and grade of dysplasia (see ).
Reflux symptoms should be controlled with PPI therapy to ensure accurate EGD surveillance.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for High-Grade Dysplasia.
feature.feature_body:
Method Advantage Disadvantage
Esophagectomy Definitive therapy Variable mortality rate 3.0% to 13% depending on institution1
Endoscopic mucosal ablation *(in conjunction with acid suppression**)
• Photodynamic therapy Decreasing cancer risk from 28% to 13% in randomized control trial2 Limited long-term data on outcomes and high rate (36%) of stricture formation2
• Thermal ablation Success rate 80-90%4 Only small cohorts of patients followed over short periods of time
• Radiofrequency ablation Success rate 70%5 Complication such as stricture formation, esophageal perforation and gastrointestinal bleeding
• Cryotherapy Resolution of high-grade dysplasia in 68% to 94% of patients in prospective trials6,7 Limited data on efficacy; only short-term follow-up; approximately only 60 institutions provide this intervention
Endoscopic mucosal resection*** Both diagnostic and therapeutic; calculated 5-year survival rate of 98%8 Recurrence rates of 11%8 and stricture formation
